While this mode has shown strong gains on complex tasks by allocating additional computation at inference time, it introduces significant latency overhead because the hidden chain 𝐜 \mathbf{c} is usually much longer than the response 𝐫 \mathbf{r} and must also be generated autoregressively. Non-Thinking Mode. In classical settings, LLMs generate the response 𝐫 \mathbf{r} directly, conditioned only on the query: 𝐫 ∼ p θ ( ⋅ ∣ 𝐪 ) . \mathbf{r}\sim p_{\theta}(\cdot\mid\mathbf{q}). (3) By sacrificing the ability to use thinking traces as a scratchpad, this mode can achieve dramatically lower latency than Thinking mode. This Non-Thinking mode can also be invoked in post-trained models by prompting with null thinking tokens ( Ma et al., 2025 ) , or by post-training with the Non-Thinking mode ( Qwen Team, 2025 ) . Note that even without thinking tokens, the response tokens 𝐫 \mathbf{r} produced in Non-Thinking mode can still include step-by-step solutions ( i.e., chain-of-thought) before emitting the answer. 3 HyperThink We introduce HyperThink , a framework that reframes thinking as query-conditioned parameter modulation of a language model rather than explicit token generation. We view the thinking process as an intermediate computation that steers the model’s decoding dynamics before producing the final response. HyperThink realizes this steering through a lightweight query-specific parameter update predicted by an amortized hypernetwork, enabling direct response generation without thinking tokens while approximating the response distribution of Thinking Mode. 3.1 Thinking Process as Parameter Updates We relate the Thinking and Non-Thinking modes from Section 2 through the lens of distribution steering. In Thinking mode, the chain of thinking tokens 𝐜 \mathbf{c} is generated from each query 𝐪 \mathbf{q} and steers the model from the direct response distribution p θ ​ ( 𝐫 ∣ 𝐪 ) p_{\theta}(\mathbf{r}\mid\mathbf{q}) toward the conditioned distribution p θ ​ ( 𝐫 ∣ 𝐪 , 𝐜 ) p_{\theta}(\mathbf{r}\mid\mathbf{q},\mathbf{c}) . Our goal is to approximate this steering effect with a query-conditioned parameter shift Δ ​ θ ​ ( 𝐪 ) \Delta\theta(\mathbf{q}) , avoiding both generation of and conditioning on the thinking tokens 𝐜 \mathbf{c} . Concretely, we posit the existence of a parameter update Δ ​ θ ​ ( 𝐪 ) \Delta\theta(\mathbf{q}) such that the Non-Thinking mode decoding of the updated model matches the Thinking mode decoding: p θ + Δ ​ θ ​ ( 𝐪 ) ​ ( 𝐫 ∣ 𝐪 ) ≈ p θ ​ ( 𝐫 ∣ 𝐪 , 𝐜 ) . p_{\theta+\Delta\theta(\mathbf{q})}(\mathbf{r}\mid\mathbf{q})\;\approx\;p_{\theta}(\mathbf{r}\mid\mathbf{q},\mathbf{c}). (4) Here, Δ ​ θ ​ ( 𝐪 ) \Delta\theta(\mathbf{q}) is intended to implicitly capture the effect of conditioning on 𝐜 \mathbf{c} , i.e. , the resulting shift in the model’s activations and KV-cache. This formulation is motivated by studies on the duality between in-context learning and fine-tuning ( Von Oswald et al., 2023 ; Dai et al., 2023 ) . A simple way to obtain Δ ​ θ ​ ( 𝐪 ) \Delta\theta(\mathbf{q}) from a query 𝐪 \mathbf{q} is to maximize the likelihood of the responses from Thinking mode under the updated model: Δ ​ θ ∗ ​ ( 𝐪 ) = argmax Δ ​ θ ∈ Θ ​ 𝔼 ( 𝐫 , 𝐜 ) ∼ p θ ( ⋅ ∣ 𝐪 ) ​ [ log ⁡ p θ + Δ ​ θ ​ ( 𝐫 ∣ 𝐪 ) ] \Delta\theta^{*}(\mathbf{q})\;=\;\underset{\Delta\theta\in\Theta}{\mathrm{argmax}}\underset{(\mathbf{r},\mathbf{c})\sim p_{\theta}(\cdot\mid\mathbf{q})}{\mathbb{E}}\left[\log p_{\theta+\Delta\theta}(\mathbf{r}\mid\mathbf{q})\right] (5) where Θ \Theta denotes the space of the LLM parameters. While Eq. ( 5 ) provides a principled way to obtain Δ ​ θ ∗ ​ ( 𝐪 ) \Delta\theta^{*}(\mathbf{q}) , it still requires generating the thinking tokens 𝐜 \mathbf{c} in addition to the optimization process for each query 𝐪 \mathbf{q} , which is computationally prohibitive at inference time and provides no benefit over Thinking Mode. We therefore amortize the mapping from queries to parameter updates by training a hypernetwork f ψ f_{\psi} that predicts Δ ​ θ \Delta\theta directly from 𝐪 \mathbf{q} : Δ ​ θ ​ ( 𝐪 ) = f ψ ​ ( 𝐪 ) , \Delta\theta(\mathbf{q})\;=\;f_{\psi}(\mathbf{q}), (6) The hypernetwork can be trained end-to-end with the maximum likelihood objective in Eq. ( 5 ). At inference, HyperThink applies the predicted parameter update from the trained hypernetwork to the frozen base model and directly generates the response tokens 𝐫 \mathbf{r} . This replaces long sequential thinking-trace generation with one non-autoregressive hypernetwork pass. The resulting method incurs a modest latency overhead over Native Non-Thinking while avoiding the substantially longer sequential decoding required by explicit thinking traces. 3.2 Bias-Only Adaptation Predicting the full weight updates Δ ​ θ \Delta\theta for LLMs with a hypernetwork, however, is impractical due to the massive ( e.g., billions) output dimensionality. We therefore restrict adaptation to a tiny subset of parameters: bias parameters of several selected transformer layers of the LLM backbone. Let 𝐛 ∈ ℝ D \mathbf{b}\in\mathbb{R}^{D} denote the concatenation of the selected bias parameters. HyperThink only predicts the shift in selected biases: Δ ​ 𝐛 ​ ( 𝐪 ) = f ψ ​ ( 𝐪 ) \Delta\mathbf{b}(\mathbf{q})=f_{\psi}(\mathbf{q}) . Then the predicted bias updates are applied to the base LLM to adapt θ \theta : θ + Δ ​ θ = θ ⊕ Δ ​ 𝐛 ​ ( 𝐪 ) , \theta+\Delta\theta=\theta\oplus\Delta\mathbf{b}(\mathbf{q}), (7) where ⊕ \oplus denotes adding Δ ​ 𝐛 ​ ( 𝐪 ) \Delta\mathbf{b}(\mathbf{q}) only to the bias subset while keeping other parameters fixed. We choose bias parameters for two reasons. First, the number of bias parameters is negligible compared to full weight matrices, making them easy to predict and apply with a lightweight hypernetwork. For example, in the instantiation we show in the experiments, we reduce the parameter space of a 0.6B model to only 90K ( 0.015 % 0.015\% ). Second, despite this constrained subspace, bias updates have been shown to effectively steer transformer backbones across diverse domains ( Zaken et al., 2022 ; Cho et al., 2024 ; Huang et al., 2025 ; Kim et al., 2025 ) . Other parameter subspaces, such as LoRA ( Hu et al., 2022 ) or Prompt Tuning ( Lester et al., 2021 ) , are also possible in principle; we study the impact of the chosen adaptation subspace in Section 4.3 . The output bias tokens U ⁡ ( 𝐪 ) U(\mathbf{q}) are decoded to final bias updates Δ ​ 𝐛 ​ ( 𝐪 ) \Delta\mathbf{b}(\mathbf{q}) by a VQ decoder that discretizes the contextualized parameter representations using a learned codebook ℰ \mathcal{E} . 3.3 Hypernetwork Architecture The hypernetwork f ψ f_{\psi} consists of three components (see Figure 2 ): a Text Encoder that embeds the query, a Bias Encoder that contextualizes a set of learnable parameter tokens with the query representation, and a VQ Decoder that discretizes the resulting representations and projects them into the target bias-update space. Text Encoder. The first stage extracts a contextual representation of the input query 𝐪 \mathbf{q} . We employ a frozen pretrained transformer ( e.g., a copy of the base LLM) to produce a sequence of text tokens: H text = Encoder text ​ ( 𝐪 ) ∈ ℝ L q × d enc , H_{\text{text}}=\mathrm{Encoder}_{\text{text}}(\mathbf{q})\in\mathbb{R}^{L_{q}\times d_{\text{enc}}}, (8) where L q L_{q} is the query length. These embeddings serve as the query context for subsequent parameter generation. By using a pretrained language model as the text encoder, we obtain robust representations that capture the semantic structure of the query relevant for predicting bias updates. Since the query length is relatively small and we only apply a single forward pass of the encoder, the cost of text encoding is substantially lower than autoregressively generating a long chain of thinking tokens, and thus does not conflict with our goal of efficient reasoning. Bias Encoder. The hypernetwork must output a structured bias update, consisting of multiple bias vectors for each layer. To explicitly represent these update slots, we introduce M M learnable bias tokens U 0 = [ u 1 ; … ; u M ] ∈ ℝ M × d hyper U_{0}=[u_{1};\dots;u_{M}]\in\mathbb{R}^{M\times d_{\text{hyper}}} , where M M is the number of layers whose biases are updated and each token u j u_{j} is assigned to a layer ℓ j \ell_{j} . Then we encode the bias tokens using an MM-DiT ( Esser et al., 2024 ) architecture, which jointly encodes the text tokens H text H_{\text{text}} and the parameter tokens U 0 U_{0} by considering them as separate modalities, with modality-specific LayerNorm/MLP and joint self-attention. This enables the model to contextualize query information into the parameters while capturing the dependencies among layer-wise parameters. We use the output parameter tokens as the contextualized representation U ⁡ ( 𝐪 ) ∈ ℝ M × d hyper U(\mathbf{q})\in\mathbb{R}^{M\times d_{\text{hyper}}} , which will be decoded into the final bias update. VQ Decoder. To regularize the update space and encourage reuse of common update patterns, we introduce a discrete bottleneck via vector quantization (VQ) with layer-wise learnable codebooks ℰ j = { e 1 j , … , e K j } ⊂ ℝ d z \mathcal{E}^{j}=\{e_{1}^{j},\dots,e_{K}^{j}\}\subset\mathbb{R}^{d_{z}} to decode the continuous outputs of the bias encoder. For each token U j ​ ( 𝐪 ) U_{j}(\mathbf{q}) , we project it to a latent z j z_{j} , quantize it to the nearest code within the corresponding codebook ℰ j \mathcal{E}^{j} , and decode it into the actual bias update Δ ​ 𝐛 ( ℓ j ) \Delta\mathbf{b}^{(\ell_{j})} for the layer. Concatenating Δ ​ 𝐛 ( ℓ j ) ​ ( 𝐪 ) \Delta\mathbf{b}^{(\ell_{j})}(\mathbf{q}) over j = 1 , … , M j=1,\dots,M yields the full bias update Δ ​ 𝐛 ​ ( 𝐪 ) ∈ ℝ D \Delta\mathbf{b}(\mathbf{q})\in\mathbb{R}^{D} . During training, we use a straight-through estimator to backpropagate through the quantization step, while learning the codebook entries jointly with the decoder. The discrete bottleneck acts as an inductive bias by constraining updates to be composed from a finite set of learned prototypes shared by queries. This reduces the effective degrees of freedom of instance-specific adaptation and makes the predicted update behave more like a reusable reasoning primitive than an unconstrained per-example perturbation. We zero-initialize the VQ decoder’s output projection ( W out , b out ) (W_{\mathrm{out}},b_{\mathrm{out}}) , ensuring Δ ​ 𝐛 ​ ( 𝐪 ) ≡ 0 \Delta\mathbf{b}(\mathbf{q})\equiv 0 and an initial match to the frozen base model. 3.4 Training Objective Figure 3: Maximum likelihood objective for HyperThink . HyperThink predicts query-specific bias parameters and injects them into the base LLM, and is trained to steer the Non-Thinking response distribution into that of Thinking mode. During training, the base parameters θ = ( θ w , 𝐛 ) \theta=(\theta_{\text{w}},\mathbf{b}) are kept frozen; we update only the hypernetwork parameters ψ \psi and the VQ codebook ℰ \mathcal{E} end-to-end. Our objective consists of (i) a maximum-likelihood term that trains HyperThink to reproduce teacher-generated responses without internal thinking tokens, (ii) a vector-quantization objective that stabilizes the discrete bottleneck, and (iii) a usage regularizer that prevents code collapse in the VQ decoder. Maximum Likelihood Objective. To encourage the hypernetwork output f ψ ​ ( 𝐪 ) f_{\psi}(\mathbf{q}) to steer the response distribution in the Non-Thinking mode toward that of the Thinking mode, we employ an end-to-end maximum likelihood (cross-entropy) objective using correctness-filtered, teacher-generated response tokens from Thinking Mode: ℒ CE ( ψ ) = 𝔼 𝐪 ∼ 𝒟 𝐫 , 𝐜 ∼ p θ ( ⋅ ∣ 𝐪 ) [ ∑ t = 1 | 𝐫 | − log p θ + Δ ​ θ ​ ( 𝐪 ) ( r t ∣ 𝐫 < t , 𝐪 ) ] , \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{CE}}(\psi)=\underset{\begin{subarray}{c}\mathbf{q}\sim\mathcal{D}\\ \mathbf{r},\mathbf{c}\sim p_{\theta}(\cdot\mid\mathbf{q})\end{subarray}}{\mathbb{E}}\left[\sum_{t=1}^{|\mathbf{r}|}-\log p_{\theta+\Delta\theta(\mathbf{q})}\bigl(r_{t}\mid\mathbf{r}_{<t},\mathbf{q}\bigr)\right], (9) where the parameter updates Δ ​ θ ​ ( 𝐪 ) \Delta\theta(\mathbf{q}) are produced by the hypernetwork f ψ f_{\psi} (Eq. Vector Quantization Objective. To learn discrete reasoning prototypes, we employ the standard VQ-VAE objective ( van den Oord et al., 2017 ) . We use a straight-through estimator to backpropagate through the non-differentiable code selection and add the auxiliary loss ℒ VQ ​ ( ψ ) = 𝔼 𝐪 ∼ 𝒟 ​ [ ∑ j = 1 M ( ‖ sg ⁡ [ z j ​ ( 𝐪 ) ] − e k j ‖ 2 2 + β ​ ‖ z j ​ ( 𝐪 ) − sg ⁡ [ e k j ] ‖ 2 2 ) ] , \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{VQ}}(\psi)=\underset{\mathbf{q}\sim\mathcal{D}}{\mathbb{E}}\Bigg[\sum_{j=1}^{M}\Big(\|\mathrm{sg}[z_{j}(\mathbf{q})]-e_{k_{j}}\|_{2}^{2}+\beta\|z_{j}(\mathbf{q})-\mathrm{sg}[e_{k_{j}}]\|_{2}^{2}\Big)\Bigg], (10) where z j ​ ( 𝐪 ) z_{j}(\mathbf{q}) is the projected latent for parameter token j j , e k j e_{k_{j}} is the selected code, sg ⁡ [ ⋅ ] \mathrm{sg}[\cdot] denotes stop-gradient, and β ∈ ℝ \beta\in\mathbb{R} is a hyperparameter. For general reasoning experiments, we use SmolLM3-3B and Olmo-3-7B-Think ( Team Olmo, 2025 ) as base models. All models are extensively post-trained for Thinking and Non-Thinking inference, and Qwen3 supports token-budget control, making them exceptionally strong baselines for HyperThink . We follow their standard decoding settings, with a temperature of 0.6 0.6 and nucleus sampling with p = 0.95 p=0.95 . For each query, we draw five samples and report the average accuracy and Pass@5 as performance metrics. To fairly assess the inference cost of our hypernetwork-based method and prompting baselines, we also report FLOPs averaged over the samples. Datasets. For the mathematical reasoning experiments, we train Qwen3-0.6B on GSM8K ( Cobbe et al., 2021 ) and SmolLM3-3B on DeepScaleR ( Luo et al., 2025 ) . Then we evaluate both models on the standard GSM8K test split as well as MATH-500 ( Hendrycks et al., 2021 ) as the out-of-domain benchmark. For the general reasoning experiments, we augment the training data with CodeForces-CoTs ( Penedo et al., 2025 ) , LogiQA ( Liu et al., 2020 ) , OpenBookQA ( Mihaylov et al., 2018 ) , and QASC ( Khot et al., 2020 ) , also covering coding, logical reasoning, and general question-answering tasks. We then evaluate the model on AIME ( Jia, 2024 ; Dekoninck et al., 2026 ) , LiveCodeBench ( Jain et al., 2025 ) , BIG-Bench Hard ( Suzgun et al., 2023 ) , and CommonsenseQA ( Talmor et al., 2019 ) , which assess Olympiad-level mathematics, code generation, multi-step reasoning, and commonsense question answering, respectively. Baselines. We compare HyperThink against five baselines: Thinking Mode , which generates an explicit reasoning trace before producing the final response; Budget-Controlled Thinking Mode , which constrains Thinking-Mode generation to a token budget comparable to that of HyperThink ; Native Non-Thinking Mode , which directly produces a response using the model’s native non-thinking configuration; System 2 Distillation ( Yu et al., 2024 ) , which uses the same training objective as HyperThink but directly fine-tunes the base LLM rather than predicting query-conditioned parameter updates; and TokenSkip ( Xia et al., 2025 ) , which learns to selectively omit less important tokens for controllable compression of reasoning traces. Full details are provided in Appendix B . Implementation Details. For the hypernetwork text encoder, we use a pretrained backbone and keep it frozen during training. The hypernetwork consists of a lightweight MM-DiT-based bias encoder and a VQ decoder. We adapt biases in the later transformer blocks of the base LLM, targeting a small subset of projection modules; the exact architectures and parameter counts for each backbone are given in Appendix C . Unless otherwise noted, all other hypernetwork and training settings are shared across backbones. We train HyperThink and the baselines with AdamW ( Loshchilov & Hutter, 2019 ) ; full optimization hyperparameters and compute details are deferred to Appendix C . 4.2 Main Results Table 1 summarizes the Qwen3-0.6B results on the mathematical-reasoning benchmarks. We observe that HyperThink generally improves over the Non-Thinking and distillation baselines with only a small increase in FLOPs. In particular, at similar compute budgets, HyperThink yields significant improvements over Budget-Controlled Thinking Mode on both benchmarks. We also observe that System 2 Distillation and TokenSkip underperform HyperThink on the out-of-distribution MATH-500 benchmark. This suggests weaker out-of-distribution generalization with less-constrained fine-tuning, whereas VQ-constrained bias adaptation preserves stronger transfer to MATH-500. On the other hand, HyperThink successfully generalizes to out-of-distribution math problems to perform reasoning without thinking tokens. In the SmolLM3-3B model, as summarized in Table 2 , the gap between HyperThink and baselines even widens. HyperThink generally outperforms the low-budget baselines with much lower FLOPs, indicating that HyperThink scales well with model size and has strong potential for practical applications. To clearly investigate the cost-performance trade-off between baselines, we plot Pass@5 against the end-to-end answering latency measured on a single NVIDIA H200 GPU in Figure 4 . Due to the lightweight computation of the hypernetwork, which is a single forward pass on the problem text, the latency of HyperThink is largely determined by the number of generated tokens. Since HyperThink learns to directly generate response tokens, it incurs latency comparable to Native Non-Thinking. Therefore, HyperThink achieves a significantly better accuracy–latency trade-off than Budget-Controlled Thinking Mode and System 2 Distillation. Moreover, HyperThink still provides a performance boost over the Native Non-Thinking Mode with a slight increase in latency, which is notable because the base Qwen3 model is already post-trained for the Non-Thinking mode with an extensive corpus over multiple training stages. Figures 5 and 6 report results for SmolLM3-3B and Olmo-3-7B-Think, respectively, with both models trained on the same mixed-domain corpus. Across CommonsenseQA and BIG-Bench Hard, HyperThink generally improves over Native Non-Thinking in the low-latency regime, showing that query-conditioned parameter updates can support reasoning beyond mathematics when the corresponding domains are covered during training. In particular, on Olmo-3-7B-Think, HyperThink achieves performance comparable to the evaluated Thinking-mode operating points on these QA benchmarks while requiring only approximately 7 7 – 9 % 9\% of their answering latency. The harder AIME and LiveCodeBench evaluations clarify the boundary of this trade-off: high-budget Thinking remains substantially stronger on search-intensive Olympiad problems, while Native Non-Thinking can remain competitive or stronger on executable code generation.
